extractions.title: May 16, 2026
extractions.publication: Letters from an American (Heather Cox Richardson)
key_claims: On May 17, 1954, the Supreme Court unanimously decided Brown v. Board of Education, declaring racial segregation in public schools unconstitutional under the Fourteenth Amendment.
Senator Strom Thurmond launched the longest filibuster in U.S. history at 24 hours and 18 minutes to prevent passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1957.
Senator Cory Booker broke Thurmond's filibuster record on March 31–April 1, 2025, speaking for 25 hours, 5 minutes, and 59 seconds, though his speech was not technically a filibuster.

Civil rights workers James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner were murdered by KKK members working with local law enforcement and buried in an earthen dam under construction near Philadelphia, Mississippi.

In Selma, Alabama, voting rolls were 99% white despite Black Americans outnumbering white Americans among the city's 29,500 residents, and a judge had banned public gatherings of more than two people to suppress voter registration.

extractions.title: I Blame My Father's Summer Reading Lists
key_claims: The author traces many of her major life choices back to summer reading lists assigned by her father, a professor of French and Francophone literature.
Her father gave her books far beyond her emotional comprehension, including Nabokov's Lolita at age twelve and works by Anaïs Nin, Paul Bowles, Fanon, Flaubert, Kafka, Camus, and Sartre.
Reading Isabelle Eberhardt's journals at fourteen profoundly shaped her relationship with the desert and sense of wanderlust.
At twenty-seven, the author embarked on a fifteen-thousand-mile solo road trip across America, which she now connects to her early reading of Eberhardt.
Her father published a biography titled 'The Immortal Journeys of Isabelle Eberhardt,' which prompted her reflection on this chain of influence.
